lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: estimating a population mean and margin of error by simulation
lessonRef.title: Targeted correction: estimating a population mean and margin of error by simulation

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Each example contains the correction, not just the answer.

items.prompt: Mean 100, sd 15. What percentage lies between 70 and 130?

steps: That is 100 ± 30, which is two standard deviations.

items.prompt: What does a randomised experiment support?

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Before solving, say which error the problem is testing for.

items.prompt: A random sample of 100 people gives a sample proportion of 21%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±20%, giving 1% to 41%
±1%, giving 20% to 22%
±10%, giving 11% to 31%
±21%, giving 0% to 42%

items.prompt: In 500 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 4 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 0.8% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 0.8% of simulations, which is not unusual.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 104 and standard deviation 9. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 86 and 122?
choices: about 99.7%
about 50%
about 68%
about 95%

items.prompt: A researcher runs a randomised controlled experiment with participants randomly assigned to treatments. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A random sample of 100 people gives a sample proportion of 33%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±1%, giving 32% to 34%
±10%, giving 23% to 43%
±33%, giving 0% to 66%
±20%, giving 13% to 53%

items.prompt: In 100 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 2 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 2% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 2% of simulations, which is not unusual.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 112 and standard deviation 14. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 84 and 140?
choices: about 95%
about 99.7%
about 68%
about 50%

items.prompt: A researcher runs a sample survey with randomly selected participants. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
